title: Listening to white groups: Red Nichols and Miff Mole
summary: Asked what modern records he followed, Waters names the Goofus Five, the Clarence Williams Five and white groups such as Red Nichols and Miff Mole, who knocked him out with their musicianship.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Bix Beiderbecke: hearing, copying and remembering him

blocks.x: Let's turn the coin over. You cited that you're up in Boston, you're starting to be able to follow the world of jazz through records, which you weren't able to do earlier, primarily because there weren't records.

among other things. But the records are available, there's a black community in Boston, you're plugged into the black musical community in Boston, and you're getting records. And you cited that you listened to this record and that record, that you didn't listen to the blues records too much -
Ah, not - excuse me, 'cause I did listen to other records before the black, I listened to white music also.
Yeah, that was the, I was tryin' to get into the -
gotta let me finish the question (laughs).

I was tryin' to say that OK, so you just told us that you didn't listen to the Bessie Smith records at this point in time. But you were interested in being an advanced musician. On the other side of the coin, what are some records illustrating the more modern sounds as you interpreted that that was on record that you listened to at that time, who were you listening to?
Well, I just got through telling you about the Goofus Five and things like that and the Clarence Williams Five. Then I listened to groups, like the white groups like Red Nichols and Miff Mole and -
Did you consider any of them particularly advanced players?
You're tellin' me, they were great! They were great!
Rather, most everything that those boys did knocked me out, because it was very, very musical.
